title: Under the hood: Future, Pin and streams
summary: The Future trait, Poll and Context, what the compiler generates for async fn, why futures must be pinned, Pin and Unpin, the Stream trait for sequences of async values, async closures and async fn in traits, and a hand-written future as an exercise.

steps.title: You write
The compiler builds a state machine
steps.md: One enum variant per suspension point, holding exactly the variables that live across it.

steps.title: poll advances it
steps.md: Each `poll` runs from the current state until the next inner future returns `Pending`, saves the state, and returns `Pending` itself. When the last step finishes, it returns `Ready`.

steps.title: Wake-ups travel up
steps.md: The innermost future (a socket, a timer) stores the waker. When the event happens it wakes it; the executor polls the outermost future, which re-enters its state machine down to the leaf.

blocks.title: Why Pin?
blocks.md:
The state machine may hold a **reference to its own data**: `let text = ...; parse(&text).await` keeps both `text` and a reference to it in the same struct. If the struct were **moved** to another address after that, the reference would point at the old location: a dangling pointer. Such types are called **self-referential**. **`Pin

`** wraps a pointer (`Pin<&mut T>`, `Pin>`) and promises that the value it points to **will not move again**. `poll` takes `self: Pin<&mut Self>`, so a future can only be polled once it is pinned, and from then on it stays put.

blocks.title: Pinning in practice
rows: a future in a local variable
`let mut f = std::pin::pin!(fut);` (pins on the stack)
a future to store or return
`Pin::new(&mut x)`: free, since moving it is harmless

blocks.title: Unpin
blocks.md: Most types do not care whether they move: integers, `String`, `Vec`, your plain structs. They implement the auto trait **`Unpin`**, and for them `Pin` is a formality. Only types that might be self-referential, chiefly the futures generated by `async`, are `!Unpin`. When an API demands `Unpin` and you have an async block, `Box::pin` it. That is why the error message for a missing pin usually suggests exactly that.

blocks.title: Writing a future by hand
blocks.md: A hand-written future is a struct with a state, and a `poll` that checks it. This `Countdown` is ready after being polled `n` times; each time it is not ready, it **wakes itself** so the executor polls it again soon, as `yield_now` does:

blocks.explain: `Countdown` holds only a `u32`, so it is `Unpin`, and `self.remaining` can be changed through the `Pin<&mut Self>` directly. A future that holds other futures (like `join2`) must poll them through pinned pointers, which is why `join2` boxed them.

blocks.title: Streams
Async closures and async fn in traits
A ticking stream
blocks.md: `Ticks` is a minimal stream: each `poll_next` yields the next number until `limit`, then `None`. `next` turns one `poll_next` into a future you can `.await`. Finish `poll_next` and sum the stream in `main` with `while let Some(n) = next(&mut ticks).await`.
hints: `if self.current >= self.limit { Poll::Ready(None) } else { self.current += 1; Poll::Ready(Some(self.current)) }`
`while let Some(n) = next(&mut ticks).await { println!("got {n}"); sum += n; }`

blocks.title: Futures by hand
blocks.goal: Implement the Future trait for your own types, write a join combinator, and drive everything with a block_on you complete yourself.
blocks.behavior:
Everything is standard library only.
- `pub fn block_on<F: Future>(fut: F) -> F::Output`: the executor from lesson 1 (a `ThreadWaker` is provided).
- `pub struct YieldN { pub left: u32 }`: a future returning `Pending` `left` times (decrementing and waking itself each time), then `Ready(())`.
- `pub struct Flag` with `pub fn new() -> (Flag, Setter)`: a future that completes with `()` once `Setter::set()` has been called (possibly from another thread). `Flag::poll` stores the waker; `set` marks the shared state done and wakes the stored waker. Use `Arc<Mutex<(bool, Option<Waker>)>>` shared by both halves.
- `pub fn join<A: Future, B: Future>(a: A, b: B) -> impl Future<Output = (A::Output, B::Output)>`: concurrent, as in lesson 2.
hints: `YieldN::poll`: `if self.left == 0 { Poll::Ready(()) } else { self.left -= 1; cx.waker().wake_by_ref(); Poll::Pending }`.
`Flag::poll`: lock the state; if done, `Ready(())`; else store `Some(cx.waker().clone())` and return `Pending`.
`Setter::set(&self)`: lock, set `done = true`, and `if let Some(w) = state.1.take() { w.wake(); }`.
`join`: `Box::pin` both futures and use `std::future::poll_fn` with two `Option` slots.
blocks.solution_explain: `Flag` and `Setter` are a one-shot notification, the core of every async channel and timer: the future stores its waker, the other side wakes it. The last test is only solvable concurrently: `second` waits on the flag that `first` sets, so a sequential join would wait forever. Locking the same mutex in `poll` and `set` avoids a lost wake-up between checking the flag and storing the waker.

questions.q: What must a future do before returning `Poll::Pending`?
options: Arrange for `cx.waker()` to be woken when it can make progress
questions.explanation: Otherwise it is never polled again.

options: Async state machines may hold references to their own fields, so they must not move once polled
questions.explanation: Moving would leave those references dangling.

options: Most ordinary types like i32, String and Vec
questions.explanation: Async-generated futures are the main exception.

questions.q: What does `Stream::poll_next` return when the stream has finished?
questions.explanation: Ready(Some(x)) for items, Ready(None) at the end.

questions.q: How do you poll a future stored in a struct field when its type is not Unpin?
questions.explanation: Box::pin pins it on the heap.

points: `Future::poll` returns `Ready(value)` or `Pending`; `Pending` comes with a promise to wake.
`async fn` becomes a state machine with a state per `.await`.
Pinning keeps self-referential futures in place; use `pin!` locally and `Box::pin` to store.
`Unpin` types can move freely; most types are `Unpin`.
A `Stream` is an async iterator: `poll_next` returns `Poll<Option<Item>>`.

terms.def: The result of polling a future: Ready with a value, or Pending.
A handle a pending future uses to tell its executor to poll it again.
The argument to poll that carries the Waker.
A pointer wrapper guaranteeing that the value it points to will not be moved.
An auto trait for types that are safe to move even after being pinned.
A type containing references to its own data, which would dangle if it moved.
An asynchronous sequence of values; the async counterpart of an iterator.
